answer.rationale: Constraints eliminate most candidates before evidence matters. rollback_release is barred by compliance regardless of memory_b1's clean record. enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) protected against an external dependency failing fast; here the write path is degrading under load, and shedding writes at settlement peak directly violates the 'do not lose customer writes' objective. regional_failover (memory_b2) fixed a latency degradation, but that was a regional fault; moving heavy write traffic mid-peak risks in-flight write loss and may just relocate a load-driven problem. add_capacity (memory_b3) is plausible but that record describes headroom provisioned BEFORE a peak; provisioning during peak rarely lands in time for a 90-minute climb. route_read_replicas (memory_b5) is the only inherited case whose symptom matches this one specifically -- primary write latency recovering once read load was moved off -- and it is reversible without touching the security patch. So I spend the single verification on memory_b5, because my whole choice rests on it and because the consolidated summary is outcome-only: it does not tell me whether read load was actually the causal driver or merely coincident with a fix, nor whether the read volume then resembles today's. All six memories are success stories with no recorded failures, which is a survivorship-shaped archive; I am treating each as 'worked once under conditions I cannot fully see' rather than as a validated rule. Value risk to flag downstream: serving reporting and reconciliation queries from replicas introduces replication lag, so settlement-adjacent figures may be read as authoritative while stale -- that must be labeled at the query layer or it will silently corrupt financial decisions, which is a worse failure than latency. Hence standard_experiment scale with explicit lag monitoring and a fast revert, not a broad rollout: if verification shows memory_b5's context diverges (e.g., the primary was read-saturated in a way today's is not), I fall back to add_capacity rather than escalating this.
